title: Forces Acting on Structures
seo_title: Grade 5 Science: Forces Acting on Structures Worksheets (Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Identify internal forces (tension, compression, torsion, shear) and external forces acting on structures; describe static and dynamic loads; explain how design, shape and materials help structures withstand forces. (summary of the Ontario Science and Technology curriculum, 2022, Strand D: Structures and Mechanisms – Forces Acting on Structures)
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 science worksheets on tension, compression, torsion and shear, loads, triangles, bridges and building safe structures. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Tension pulls, compression squeezes, torsion twists and shear slides; good designs spread forces.
body_html:
How to think about it

Forces act on every structure, from outside (external) and inside (internal).

  • External forces: weight, wind, snow, people, earthquakes. Static loads stay the same; dynamic loads change.
  • Internal forces: tension (pull), compression (squeeze), torsion (twist), shear (slide across).
  • Triangles, arches, wide bases, deep foundations and strong materials help structures stay up.
Example

Which force acts on a rope holding a swing?

the rope is pulled

Answer: tension

Example

Why are triangles used in towers?

they do not change shape

Answer: they are rigid and spread forces

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up tension and compression.
  • Thinking a taller structure is always stronger.
  • Thinking only heavy objects put forces on structures (wind and snow do too).

faq.q: What is the difference between tension and compression?
faq.a: Tension is a pulling force that stretches. Compression is a pushing force that squeezes.

faq.q: What is the difference between static and dynamic loads?
faq.a: A static load does not change, like the weight of a bridge. A dynamic load changes, like traffic or wind.
To make sure they are safe and can hold the loads they will face, such as heavy snow in an Ontario winter.

items.q: A boat floats still on a calm lake. It stays still. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced?
c: Only gravity acts, so there is no answer.
There are no forces at all.
items.e: When motion changes (start, stop, speed up, slow down, turn), forces are unbalanced. When nothing changes, they are balanced.

items.q: A girl pushes a swing. The swing starts moving. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced?
c: Only gravity acts, so there is no answer.
There are no forces at all.
items.e: When motion changes (start, stop, speed up, slow down, turn), forces are unbalanced. When nothing changes, they are balanced.

items.q: Which structure is a frame structure?
c: a hydro tower made of steel beams
items.e: Frames are joined parts with spaces between.

items.q: What is a shell structure?
c: a thin, curved outer layer that holds its shape
items.e: Eggs, domes and canoes are shell structures.

items.q: Which bridge design uses an arch to carry loads by compression?
c: a suspension bridge with no towers
items.e: The arch pushes loads to its ends.

items.q: Which material is strong in compression but weak in tension?
items.e: Concrete is reinforced with steel bars (rebar).

items.q: A laptop on a desk is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: Gravity pulls it down and the desk pushes it up with an equal force.
The forces on it are unbalanced.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: What is a dynamic (live) load?
c: the weight of the roof beams
a load that changes or moves, like traffic or wind
items.e: Dynamic loads change.

items.q: A plant pot on a windowsill is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: Gravity pulls it down and the windowsill pushes it up with an equal force.
The forces on it are unbalanced.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: A picture hangs on a nail on the wall. It stays still. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced?
c: Only gravity acts, so there is no answer.
There are no forces at all.
items.e: When motion changes (start, stop, speed up, slow down, turn), forces are unbalanced. When nothing changes, they are balanced.

items.q: What is a structure?
c: something built to hold or support a load
items.e: Buildings, bridges, chairs and nests are structures.

items.q: A steel beam has a heavy load in the middle. Which part is in tension?
items.e: The top squeezes and the bottom stretches.

items.q: How can you make a paper column hold more books?
items.e: Tubes resist compression well.

items.q: A cup on a table is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: Gravity pulls it down and the table pushes it up with an equal force.
The forces on it are unbalanced.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: A toy on a bed is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: Gravity pulls it down and the bed pushes it up with an equal force.
The forces on it are unbalanced.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: A rock on the ground is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: Gravity pulls it down and the ground pushes it up with an equal force.
The forces on it are unbalanced.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: A soccer ball is sitting still. A player kicks it. It starts moving. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced?
c: There are no forces at all.
Only gravity acts, so there is no answer.
items.e: When motion changes (start, stop, speed up, slow down, turn), forces are unbalanced. When nothing changes, they are balanced.

items.q: A bike rider squeezes the brakes. The bike slows down. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced?
c: There are no forces at all.
Only gravity acts, so there is no answer.
items.e: When motion changes (start, stop, speed up, slow down, turn), forces are unbalanced. When nothing changes, they are balanced.

items.q: A ball on the floor is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: Gravity pulls it down and the floor pushes it up with an equal force.
The forces on it are unbalanced.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: A hockey puck is hit with a stick. It speeds up. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced?
c: There are no forces at all.
Only gravity acts, so there is no answer.
items.e: When motion changes (start, stop, speed up, slow down, turn), forces are unbalanced. When nothing changes, they are balanced.

items.q: Which internal force acts on the cables of a suspension bridge?
items.e: The cables of a suspension bridge: the cables are pulled tight, so it is tension (a pulling or stretching force).

items.q: What is a static (dead) load?
c: a load that does not change, like the weight of the structure itself
items.e: Static loads stay the same.

items.q: Which of these is a contact force?
items.e: Contact forces act only when objects touch. Non-contact forces (gravitational, magnetic, electrostatic) act at a distance.

items.q: Which structure is a solid structure?
items.e: Solid structures are filled all the way through.

items.q: Why is it safer to put heavy items on the bottom shelf?
c: It lowers the centre of gravity so the shelf is less likely to tip.
items.e: Low centre of gravity improves stability.

items.q: Which internal force acts on a key turning in a lock?
items.e: A key turning in a lock: it is twisted, so it is torsion (a twisting force).

items.q: Which internal force acts on a shelf sagging under heavy books?
items.e: A shelf sagging under heavy books: it is pushed down in the middle, so it is bending (a mix of compression and tension that bends a material).

items.q: What should engineers think about when building a structure?
c: safety, strength, cost, the environment and how it will be used
items.e: Good design balances many criteria.

items.q: Which internal force acts on paper being cut by scissors?
items.e: Paper being cut by scissors: two forces push in opposite directions across it, so it is shear (two forces pushing in opposite directions across a material).

items.q: Which internal force acts on a rope holding up a swing?
items.e: A rope holding up a swing: the rope is being pulled from both ends, so it is tension (a pulling or stretching force).

items.q: What is a solid structure?
c: a structure made of solid material all the way through
items.e: Dams and brick walls are solid structures.

items.q: Is friction a contact force or a non-contact force?
items.e: Gravity (weight), magnetism and electrostatic forces act at a distance; the others need contact.

items.q: What is the name of the force from the air that pushes against a moving object?
items.e: Learn the names of common forces.

items.q: What is the name of the force of gravity pulling an object towards the Earth?
items.e: Learn the names of common forces.

items.q: Which of these is a non-contact force?
items.e: Contact forces act only when objects touch. Non-contact forces (gravitational, magnetic, electrostatic) act at a distance.

items.q: Which internal force acts on the legs of a chair with someone sitting on it?
items.e: The legs of a chair with someone sitting on it: the legs are squeezed, so it is compression (a squeezing or pushing force).

items.q: Which internal force acts on a screwdriver turning a screw?
items.e: A screwdriver turning a screw: it is twisted, so it is torsion (a twisting force).

items.q: What is a frame structure?
c: a structure made of parts joined together, like a skeleton
a solid block like a dam
items.e: Houses and bicycles have frames.

items.q: What is the name of the force of water slowing a swimmer?
items.e: Learn the names of common forces.

items.q: Which internal force acts on a guitar string?
items.e: A guitar string: the string is stretched, so it is tension (a pulling or stretching force).

items.q: A goalkeeper catches a ball flying towards the goal. Which effect of a force does this show?
c: It changes the direction of a moving object.
It makes a moving object speed up.
It makes a moving object slow down or stop.
items.e: It makes a moving object slow down or stop.

items.q: A cyclist is moving and there is a net force backwards. What happens?
c: It starts to move to the left.
It keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction.
items.e: Balanced forces: no change in motion. Unbalanced forces: speeding up, slowing down or changing direction.

items.q: A soccer is still and there is a net force to the left. What happens?
c: It starts to move to the left.
It keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction.
items.e: Balanced forces: no change in motion. Unbalanced forces: speeding up, slowing down or changing direction.

items.q: A car is moving and there is a net force backwards. What happens?
c: It starts to move to the left.
items.e: Balanced forces: no change in motion. Unbalanced forces: speeding up, slowing down or changing direction.

items.q: A bus driver presses the accelerator. Which effect of a force does this show?
c: It changes the direction of a moving object.
It makes a moving object speed up.
It changes the shape of an object.
items.e: It makes a moving object speed up.

items.q: A car is still and the forces on it are balanced. What happens?
c: It keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction.
It starts to move to the left.
items.e: Balanced forces: no change in motion. Unbalanced forces: speeding up, slowing down or changing direction.

items.q: The sled is at rest. What will happen?
c: It will move to the left.
It will move to the right.
items.e: Balanced forces do not change the motion of an object at rest.

items.q: In a tug-of-war, the Blue Team has 3 kids and the Green Team has 2 kids. Every kid pulls equally hard. What happens to the rope?
c: It moves toward the Green Team.
It moves toward the Blue Team.
items.e: The Blue Team pulls with more force, so the forces are unbalanced.

items.q: In a tug-of-war, the Blue Team has 4 kids and the Green Team has 5 kids. Every kid pulls equally hard. What happens to the rope?
c: It moves toward the Green Team.
It moves toward the Blue Team.
items.e: The Green Team pulls with more force, so the forces are unbalanced.

items.q: The sled is at rest. The arrows show two forces. What will happen?
c: It will start to move to the left.
It will start to move to the right.
It will move up into the air.
items.e: The bigger force points to the left, so the forces are unbalanced and the sled moves that way.

items.q: A soccer is still and the forces on it are balanced. What happens?
c: It keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction.
It starts to move to the left.
items.e: Balanced forces: no change in motion. Unbalanced forces: speeding up, slowing down or changing direction.

items.q: A pupil bends a plastic ruler. Which effect of a force does this show?
c: It changes the direction of a moving object.
It makes a moving object speed up.
It changes the shape of an object.
It makes a moving object slow down or stop.
items.e: It changes the shape of an object.

items.q: Two forces act on a toy car that is at rest. One arrow is longer. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced?
items.e: The forces are not equal, so they are unbalanced.

items.q: In a tug-of-war, the Green Team has 5 kids and the Red Team has 5 kids. Every kid pulls equally hard. What happens to the rope?
c: It moves toward the Green Team.
It breaks because there are no forces.
It moves toward the Red Team.
It does not move, because the pulls are balanced.
items.e: Equal pulls in opposite directions are balanced forces.

items.q: The chair is at rest. The arrows show two forces. What will happen?
c: It will move up into the air.
It will start to move to the left.
It will start to move to the right.
items.e: The bigger force points to the right, so the forces are unbalanced and the chair moves that way.

items.q: Two forces act on a wagon that is at rest. One arrow is longer. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced?
items.e: The forces are not equal, so they are unbalanced.

items.q: Two forces act on a crate that is at rest. One arrow is longer. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced?
items.e: The forces are not equal, so they are unbalanced.

items.q: A cyclist squeezes the brakes. Which effect of a force does this show?
c: It changes the direction of a moving object.
It makes a moving object speed up.
It changes the shape of an object.
It makes a moving object slow down or stop.
items.e: It makes a moving object slow down or stop.

items.q: In a tug-of-war, the Green Team has 2 kids and the Red Team has 5 kids. Every kid pulls equally hard. What happens to the rope?
c: It moves toward the Green Team.
It moves toward the Red Team.
items.e: The Red Team pulls with more force, so the forces are unbalanced.

items.q: In a tug-of-war, the Green Team has 3 kids and the Blue Team has 6 kids. Every kid pulls equally hard. What happens to the rope?
c: It moves toward the Blue Team.
It moves toward the Green Team.
items.e: The Blue Team pulls with more force, so the forces are unbalanced.

items.q: A door is pushed open at its handle. Which effect of a force is shown?
c: It exerts a pressure on a small area.
It makes a stationary object move.
It changes the size of an object.
items.e: Forces can change motion, shape or size, cause turning and exert pressure.

items.q: Which force pulls objects toward Earth?
items.e: Gravity pulls everything down toward Earth.

items.q: Zoe took apart building A and built B. Could Zoe have used all the same blocks?
c: No. A looks taller, so it has more blocks.
No. B looks bigger, so it has more blocks.
No. Blocks disappear when you take them apart.
items.e: Count both: 5 and 5. Same pieces, new shape.

items.q: Hana took apart building A and built B. Could Hana have used all the same blocks?
c: No. B looks bigger, so it has more blocks.
No. Blocks disappear when you take them apart.
No. A looks taller, so it has more blocks.
items.e: Count both: 10 and 10. Same pieces, new shape.

items.q: Which force slows a sliding object?
items.e: Friction acts where surfaces rub.

items.q: Which is a push?
c: lifting a bag by its handle
items.e: Pressing moves something away from you.

items.q: Which internal force acts on a bungee cord when someone jumps?
items.e: A bungee cord when someone jumps: it is stretched, so it is tension (a pulling or stretching force).

items.q: A drawing pin is pushed into a notice board. Which effect of a force is shown?
c: It exerts a pressure on a small area.
It changes the speed of a moving object.
It makes a stationary object move.
items.e: Forces can change motion, shape or size, cause turning and exert pressure.

items.q: A cyclist pedals harder to go up a slope. Which effect of a force is shown?
c: It changes the direction of a moving object.
It changes the speed of a moving object.
It changes the shape of an object.
items.e: Forces can change motion, shape or size, cause turning and exert pressure.

items.q: What can unbalanced forces do to an object?
c: start it, stop it, speed it up, slow it down or change its direction
items.e: Unbalanced forces change motion.

items.q: What is a force?
c: a kind of energy you can eat
items.e: Kicks, lifts and tugs are all forces.

items.q: Why do tall buildings sway a little in strong wind?
c: They are designed to bend slightly instead of breaking.
items.e: Flexibility absorbs force.

items.q: Which is an external force on a house?
items.e: External forces act on a structure from outside.

items.q: A spring is pulled and gets longer. Which effect of a force is shown?
c: It changes the shape of an object.
It makes a stationary object move.
It changes the size of an object.
items.e: Forces can change motion, shape or size, cause turning and exert pressure.

items.q: Which shape is the weakest if pushed at a corner: a square frame or a triangle frame?
items.e: Squares can fold into a diamond shape.

items.q: Two kids push a box from opposite sides with equal force. What happens?
items.e: The forces are balanced.

items.q: Why do bridges have expansion joints?
c: Materials expand in summer heat and shrink in winter cold.
To make the bridge longer every day
items.e: Joints stop cracking.

items.q: Which internal force acts on a bolt holding two sliding plates together?
items.e: A bolt holding two sliding plates together: the plates push it sideways in opposite directions, so it is shear (two forces pushing in opposite directions across a material).

items.q: Benjamin took apart building A and built B. Could Benjamin have used all the same blocks?
c: No. B looks bigger, so it has more blocks.
No. A looks taller, so it has more blocks.
No. Blocks disappear when you take them apart.
items.e: Count both: 9 and 9. Same pieces, new shape.

items.q: Which natural structure is a shell?
items.e: Turtle shells are curved and strong.

items.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
c: Weight is measured in kg and mass in N.
Mass is the amount of matter in an object (kg); weight is the gravitational force on it (N).
Mass changes on the Moon but weight does not.
items.e: On the Moon your mass is the same, but your weight is less.

items.q: Why is steel rebar put inside concrete?
c: Steel resists tension, so the concrete does not crack when it bends.
items.e: Reinforced concrete is strong both ways.

items.q: Why do astronauts bounce around on the Moon?
c: There is no gravity at all.
Their weight is less because the Moon's gravity is weaker.
The Moon is made of springs.
items.e: Weaker gravitational field.

items.q: Noah pushes a heavy box but it does not move. Why?
c: Friction pushes back with the same force, so the forces are balanced.
items.e: Balanced forces do not change motion.

items.q: Why is it easier to loosen a nut with a long spanner than a short one?
c: A force further from the pivot gives a larger turning effect.
items.e: Pushing far from the pivot helps.

items.q: Emma hung a stone on a spring scale. It read 6 N. She lowered the stone into water and it read 4 N. What can she conclude?
c: Water pushed up on the stone with a force of 2 N.

items.q: Priya wants to test how the size of a push changes how far a ball rolls. What should she change?
c: only the size of the push
items.e: Change one variable for a fair test.

items.q: Nathan hangs a weight from a spring. The spring stretches, then stops. Why does the weight stop moving?
c: The spring pulls up with the same force as gravity pulls down.
items.e: The forces become balanced.

items.q: Which internal force acts on a wet towel being wrung out?
items.e: A wet towel being wrung out: it is twisted, so it is torsion (a twisting force).

items.q: Why does a ship float?
c: The upthrust from the water balances its weight.
Water pulls it up with magnets.
items.e: Balanced forces.

items.q: Does a car moving at a steady speed on a flat road need a net force?
c: No. The driving force balances friction and air resistance.
items.e: Newton's first law.

items.q: An astronaut goes from the Earth to the Moon. What happens?
c: Her mass and weight both decrease.
Her mass decreases but her weight stays the same.
Her mass stays the same but her weight decreases.
items.e: Gravity on the Moon is weaker.

items.q: A pupil wants to compare forces fairly. Why should he use the same spring scale each time?
c: so that the force is smaller
so that the readings can be compared accurately
items.e: Different balances may read differently.

items.q: A bookshelf wobbles side to side. What could make it more stable?
c: add a diagonal brace to make triangles
stack heavy books on the top shelf
items.e: Diagonals stop racking.

items.q: Why should a spring scale read 0 N before an object is hung on it?
c: to make sure the reading is accurate
so the spring does not stretch
items.e: Check the zero first.

items.q: Aiden pulled a toy cart with a spring scale. It read 3 N on a smooth floor and 7 N on carpet. Why?
c: There is more friction on carpet.
The cart is heavier on carpet.
items.e: Rougher surfaces give more friction.

items.q: What happens to a moving object when the forces on it are balanced?
c: It keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction.
items.e: Balanced forces do not change motion.

items.q: Wind pushes hard on the side of a tall sign. What kind of force is this?
items.e: Wind changes and acts from outside.

items.q: Ava pushes a toy car gently and then hard. Which push makes it move farther?
items.e: A bigger force changes motion more.

items.q: Which internal force acts on the bricks at the bottom of a wall?
items.e: The bricks at the bottom of a wall: the weight above squeezes them, so it is compression (a squeezing or pushing force).
